subject: Computer Networking
title: NFC: Tap to Connect
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on NFC: Tap to Connect.

hook.text: You tap your phone on a payment terminal. Money transfers in a fraction of a second. That's NFC.

buildup.text: NFC works at ranges of just a few centimeters. The proximity itself acts as a security measure.

discovery.text: NFC uses electromagnetic induction. The reader generates a field; the tag or device responds with data.

twist.text: NFC tags are passive — they have no battery. The reader's field powers them. That's why stickers and cards work.

climax.text: Apple Pay, Google Pay, transit cards, and hotel key cards all use NFC. Tap-to-do-anything is now mainstream.

punchline.text: NFC: close enough to touch, fast enough to forget.

quiz.question: How do passive NFC tags work without a battery?
options: They draw power from the reader's electromagnetic field
They store solar energy during the day
They use the phone's battery wirelessly

details.summary: Near Field Communication enables devices to exchange data by touching or bringing them within a few centimeters. NFC powers contactless payments, transit cards, access badges, and device pairing.
details.whyItMatters: NFC has become the standard for contactless payments worldwide. Its intentional short range creates a simple, intuitive interaction: tap to pay, tap to pair, tap to share.
takeaways: NFC operates within about 4 centimeters at 13.56 MHz
Contactless payments use NFC with secure element encryption
Passive NFC tags require no battery and cost pennies each

faq.question: How do contactless payments work with NFC?
faq.answer: The phone or card communicates with the payment terminal over NFC. A secure element or host card emulation generates a one-time token representing the card. The token is transmitted instead of the actual card number. The terminal sends the token to the payment network for authorization.

faq.question: What are NFC tags used for?
faq.answer: NFC tags are small passive chips that transmit stored data when a phone touches them. Museums use them for exhibit information. Products use them for authentication. Smart home setups use them to trigger automations. Businesses use them for links to websites or Wi-Fi credentials.
